html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. ZDR: zero data retention; BAA: business associate agreement

  • The Claude model tiers and what each is for
  • The trade-offs: capability, latency, cost, context, availability
  • Effort, thinking and fast mode as tuning levers
  • Routing and cascades across tiers
  • How to justify a choice with evals and pin it for production

2The Tiers and the Levers

Running case

Lumen Advisory Picks Models for a Bank's Three Workloads

  • Intent classification of 2 million messages a day, answers needed in under a second
  • Drafting replies from policy, moderate volume, quality matters
  • Quarterly regulatory analysis across hundreds of pages, run overnight, correctness-critical
Tier (as of 8 Nov 2026) [Verify live] Positioning Latency Price per MTok in / out Default effort
Fable 5.1 Demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work Slower $10 / $50 high
Opus 5.5 Long-running agentic coding and knowledge work; start here for most workloads Moderate $4 / $20 medium
Sonnet 5.5 Best combination of speed and intelligence Fast $2 / $10 high
Haiku 5.5 High-volume, latency-sensitive tasks: classification, extraction, routing Fastest from $0.10 / $0.50 medium

  • All current models: 1M-token context window, text and image input, 128K max output (synchronous), reliable knowledge cutoff June 2026.
  • Pricing levers: Batch API 50% off; cache reads cost 10% of base input (5% on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, 2.5% on Fable 5.1); cache writes 1.25x (5-minute) or 2x (1-hour).
  • Effort (low to max) is a behavioral signal that trades thoroughness for tokens, latency and cost; adaptive thinking lets the model decide how much to think.
  • Fast mode buys higher output speed at premium pricing on supported models.
  • Model IDs are pinned snapshots: pin the full ID in production, test before moving, and plan for retirement dates (Anthropic-operated platforms: not sooner than 2027) [Dates].
  • Platforms: Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry, Claude Platform on AWS. Availability, regional endpoints and compliance differ by platform (Module 14).
Exam tip

Questions give a binding constraint (latency, cost, quality, compliance) and ask for the tier or lever. Name the tier by the role (classification = light, general = balanced, hard reasoning = strong).

3Making the Choice

Workload Likely choice Why
High-volume classification, extraction, routing Haiku (low effort) Latency and cost dominate; the task is bounded
Customer-facing drafting, summarization Sonnet Quality and speed balanced
Complex analysis, agentic coding, long documents Opus Reasoning depth pays off
Hardest problems where evals on Opus at high effort still fail Fable Highest capability; accept latency and cost
Non-urgent bulk jobs Any tier through Batch 50% saving when latency does not matter
  • Evals decide. Choose the smallest model that passes your eval; "always the largest" and "always the smallest" are both wrong.
  • Routing: a cheap classifier (or Haiku) sends easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a larger model.
  • Cascade: try the cheap model first and escalate on low confidence or failed validation.
  • Tune before upgrading: better prompt, retrieval or examples, then effort, then model tier.
  • Retest on every model change: behavior and prompts can shift; run regression evals.
  • Match context needs: a 1M window does not replace retrieval for very large corpora (Module 9).

4Trade-Off Table

If you need... Pull this lever Cost of the lever
Lower latency Smaller tier, lower effort, streaming, caching, shorter output Possible quality loss
Lower cost Smaller tier, caching, batch, shorter prompts, routing Latency (batch) or quality
Higher quality Stronger tier, higher effort, thinking, better retrieval Cost and latency
Compliance Platform and region choice, ZDR or BAA eligible features Feature availability, setup
Stability Pinned snapshot, regression evals Delayed access to improvements
Exam tip

The smallest model that passes the eval wins; "always the largest" and "always the smallest" are both distractors.

Exam tip

Tune in order: prompt and retrieval, then effort, then tier; pin the model ID and retest on every change.

5Exam Q&A

S1A bank classifies two million messages per day into 12 intents with a sub-second target. Which choice fits best?

  • AThe balanced tier with extended thinking enabled on every request
  • BA multi-agent system with one agent per intent
  • CThe most capable tier at maximum effort for the best accuracy on every one of the two million messages
  • DThe fastest, lowest-cost tier at low effort, validated against an eval set
Show the answer

Answer: D. Bounded, high-volume, latency-sensitive classification is the light tier's role.

S2An overnight regulatory analysis is correctness-critical and latency does not matter. Which combination is best?

  • AA synchronous multi-agent run during business hours so that analysts can watch it progress live
  • BA strong tier at higher effort, run through the Batch API for the 50 percent saving
  • CThe fastest tier in streaming mode for a responsive experience
  • DThe smallest tier at low effort to minimize the bill
Show the answer

Answer: B. Quality-first model with batch discounts suits non-urgent, critical work.

S3A team wants to save cost without hurting quality. What is the best method?

  • ARun an eval, then move to the smallest tier that still passes the quality bar
  • BSwitch tiers weekly and keep whichever one feels better to the team during that particular week
  • CKeep the largest tier and shorten the system prompt
  • DMove all traffic to the smallest tier at once and monitor customer complaints to see if quality drops
Show the answer

Answer: A. Evals prove the cheaper tier is good enough.

S4Why should a production system pin the full model ID?

  • APinned IDs increase the context window
  • BPinned IDs are cheaper than aliases because Anthropic bills a lower rate for any pinned snapshot
  • CPinned IDs disable retirement of the model
  • DBehavior is tied to a specific snapshot, so changes should be tested and rolled out deliberately
Show the answer

Answer: D. Pinning gives stability; move only after regression evals.

S5A router sends easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a large model. Which benefit does this give?

  • AAutomatic retirement of the large model
  • BElimination of the need for evals
  • CGuaranteed identical answers from both models, so that results never differ between easy and hard cases
  • DLower average cost and latency while keeping quality where it is needed
Show the answer

Answer: D. Routing aligns capability and cost with task difficulty, so average cost and latency fall while hard cases still get the stronger model.

S6Which TWO levers reduce latency for an interactive assistant? Select TWO.

  • ARouting every request through the Batch API
  • BStreaming the response so users see output early
  • CRaising effort to maximum
  • DAdding more few-shot examples to the prompt without limit
  • EA smaller tier or lower effort for routine turns
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. Streaming improves perceived latency; smaller tier and lower effort cut generation time.

S7Evals on the balanced tier fail on the hardest 10 percent of cases even after prompt and retrieval improvements. What is the next step?

  • ATest a stronger tier or higher effort on those cases, perhaps via cascade or routing
  • BReplace the model with a rules engine for all cases
  • CRemove the hardest cases from the eval set so that the stronger tier is never needed for production
  • DLower the pass threshold to match current results
Show the answer

Answer: A. Step up only on evidence, ideally for just the hard slice.

6Quick Reference Card
